editorNote: This issue follows the October magazine rack: home-computer gaming is becoming a how-to subject, the Commodore 64 is technical enough to need memory maps, and store counters still sell Apple II business disks beside Atari and VIC-20 play.
morningLine: On the radio, John Cougar holds No. 1; at theaters, E.T. retakes the weekend; on the computer shelf, October magazines turn game making into a practical lesson.

lead.headline: COMPUTE! Turns Game Making Into the Main Story
lead.summary: COMPUTE!'s October 1982 issue put "The Computer Games Of Tomorrow" and programming games with limited memory on the same cover rack as Atari, VIC-20, Apple, Sinclair/Timex, and Commodore 64 material. For this week's Chronicle, that magazine shelf is the cleanest signal: home-computer games were no longer just boxed products, but lessons, listings, reviews, and experiments for readers ready to type, tune, and modify their own software.
lead.confidence: October 1982 magazine issue used as same-month shelf context for the week of October 11-17

computerItems.headline: Games Become a Programming Curriculum
computerItems.summary: COMPUTE! paired game-design articles with type-in programs and reviews, making play a route into BASIC, memory limits, graphics, and machine-language curiosity.

computerItems.headline: C64 Memory Map Reaches New Owners
computerItems.summary: The same issue included a Commodore 64 memory-map feature, a sign that the new 64K machine was moving from showroom promise to hands-on exploration.

computerItems.headline: Atari Games Get Review Space
computerItems.summary: Four Atari games and Turtile Pilot for the Atari appeared in the October issue mix, keeping the 8-bit Atari line visible beside Apple, PET, VIC, and Sinclair/Timex coverage.

computerItems.label: Office Counter
computerItems.headline: VisiCalc Still Explains the Business Micro
computerItems.summary: Even as games filled the rack, VisiCalc remained the familiar answer for buyers asking why a personal computer belonged in an office.

market.headline: Magazine Shelves Sell the Home-Computer Future
market.summary: The October rack mixes programming lessons, reviews, utilities, education, speech synthesis, modem notes, and new-products blurbs. That blend captures late-1982 computing: users bought machines, then bought magazines to discover what the machines could become.

bbsNote.headline: Modem Desk: Telegaming Enters the Vocabulary
bbsNote.summary: COMPUTE! listed a telecommunications item titled "Telegaming," a period reminder that games and modems were already being imagined together before home networking was common.

curiosity.headline: At the Movies: E.T. Retakes the Weekend
curiosity.summary: For the October 15 weekend, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial led the domestic box office, narrowly ahead of An Officer and a Gentleman, with My Favorite Year in third.

briefs.headline: Jack & Diane Holds No. 1
briefs.summary: John Cougar led the Billboard Hot 100 dated October 16, 1982, with Men at Work, the Alan Parsons Project, Chicago, and Steve Miller Band filling out the top five.

briefs.headline: My Favorite Year Stays in the Top Three
briefs.summary: The comedy sat third on the October 15 domestic weekend chart, behind E.T. and An Officer and a Gentleman.

briefs.headline: C64 Technical Notes Hit Print
briefs.summary: A Commodore 64 memory-map article in COMPUTE! shows early owners needing practical maps of the new machine.
